1: \section{What confidence transport did in the nonlinear study}
2: \label{sec:transport-followup}
3: 
4: Does a valid way to transport confidence also give useful decisions and
5: informative regret bounds?  We study this question in a controlled nonlinear
6: model.  Cumulative pseudo-regret measures the expected reward lost, over all
7: rounds, by choosing the learner's action instead of the best action for each
8: context.  Lower values are better.  In this study, the Hessian policy
9: has higher mean pseudo-regret than every comparator in every condition.
10: Its regret bounds, and those of the frozen reference policy, are larger than
11: a simple deterministic cap.  The recorded confidence and optimism checks
12: nevertheless pass.  The findings separate those numerical checks from the
13: practical usefulness of the resulting scores and bounds.
14: 
15: The prespecified follow-up evaluates 600 policy trajectories; a separate 294
16: development and tuning trajectories precede evaluation.  We fix
17: $T=1000$ and $W\in\{16,1,0.25\}$, with 50 common evaluation seeds per condition
18: and four policies.  The model parameter $W$ changes both the reward function
19: and its curvature, so comparisons across conditions do not isolate an effect
20: of metric drift.  The original near-linear study appears separately in
21: \Cref{sec:transport-instantiation}; its evidence is not pooled with this study.
22: 
23: \paragraph{What differs between the policies?}
24: All policies use the corrected center and confidence radius from
25: \Cref{cor:corrected-center-new}.  They differ in how they turn a width into an
26: exploration bonus.  \emph{Hessian} inflates the current width using the analytic
27: path certificate $\bar D_t^Q$.  \emph{Endpoint} replaces that path certificate
28: with the dense endpoint Thompson distance.  \emph{Frozen reference} uses the
29: reference width directly.  \emph{Naive current} uses the current width without
30: transport and serves as an uncertified control.  All four policies update
31: their representations: ``frozen'' describes the metric's collection-time
32: gradients, not a fixed representation.  The policies receive matched contexts
33: and potential-noise streams, but their actions and subsequent learning
34: histories can differ.
35: 
36: \paragraph{Which policies incur less regret?}
37: \Cref{fig:transport-followup-outcomes} shows the higher mean regret of Hessian
38: transport in each condition; \Cref{tab:transport-followup-outcomes} gives the
39: numerical values.  The paired comparisons ask how much a comparator's regret
40: differs from Hessian's on the same evaluation seed.  All nine paired 95\%
41: intervals for this difference exclude zero in the comparator's favor.
42: These are pointwise intervals from 10,000 paired seed-bootstrap resamples per
43: comparison, without multiplicity adjustment.  They describe evaluation-seed
44: variation for the fixed teacher, design, and selected optimizer; they do not
45: include uncertainty from choosing the environment or tuning the optimizer.
46: Because policies follow their own adaptive histories, this comparison
47: measures the outcome of each complete policy.  It does not isolate the
48: effect of changing only a certificate at a fixed state or establish a
49: universal policy ordering.
50: 
51: For descriptive context, the online context-free mean-only benchmark has mean
52: regrets 185.26, 183.06, and 176.67 at $W=16,1,0.25$, respectively; the best fixed
53: action in hindsight has mean regrets 180.01, 177.97, and 171.84.  These means
54: use the same evaluation streams.  Hessian's sample means are close to the
55: context-free benchmark's, but no equivalence test was performed.  Similar
56: regret does not imply matching actions or identical use of context, and these
57: benchmarks do not bound the benefit available to another context-dependent
58: policy.  \Cref{app:transport-followup} defines both benchmarks.
59:

64:   condition.  Left: descriptive mean cumulative pseudo-regret at $T=1000$,

74: 
75: \paragraph{Do the regret bounds give useful information?}
76: We judge these regret bounds by whether they improve on what the reward
77: range already guarantees.  That range gives the deterministic regret cap
78: $2T\min(1,\sqrt W)$, which is 2000, 2000, and 1000 for the three conditions.
79: We call a larger bound \emph{vacuous}: it adds no information beyond the cap.
80: Every Hessian-policy bound is vacuous.  The frozen policy's own
81: reference-geometry bounds also exceed the caps in all 150 of its trajectories.
82: \Cref{fig:transport-followup-bound-scale} shows the size of their mean
83: right-hand sides relative to the cap.  The frozen policy's mean bounds are
84: much smaller than Hessian's, but neither provides a useful regret upper bound
85: in this study.
86: 
87: The largest contribution to the Hessian bounds is path inflation, the extra
88: charge introduced by the path certificate, in all three conditions.  This
89: explains their scale within the bound calculation, but
90: removing that term from Hessian's histories would not give the bound or
91: outcome of the frozen policy: the latter follows different histories.
92: The original near-linear study instead reported base-term dominance; that
93: description does not apply to this follow-up.
94:

120: \paragraph{What did the confidence and drift checks show?}
121: The unfavorable policy outcomes did not coincide with a recorded failure of
122: the confidence or optimism checks.  The former check whether the reference
123: bands contain the true mean rewards; the latter check whether the action
124: scores upper-bound those means.  All 600 evaluation trajectories,
125: including naive current, pass the simultaneous reference-confidence,
126: method-optimism, and deterministic diagnostics.  Each policy--condition cell
127: has 50 successes out of 50, with an exact 95\% Clopper--Pearson interval of
128: approximately $[92.9\%,100\%]$.  These are observed checks, not proof of
129: population coverage or of the need for transport.  Float64 checks and
130: converged quadrature are numerical diagnostics; they do not verify the
131: theorem's assumptions through rigorous numerical enclosures.
132: 
133: There is measurable movement between the reference and current matrices.
134: The primary policy reaches endpoint distances above one in 16 of 50 seeds at
135: $W=0.25$, including 286 of 50,000 seed--round observations
136: (\Cref{tab:transport-followup-drift-bounds}).  These round counts describe
137: dependent observations, not additional independent replications.  The target
138: labels used to encode $W$ are not measured endpoint distances.
139: 
140: \paragraph{Model and implementation details.}
141: The observations are Gaussian with mean
142: $\mu_{\btheta}(z)=\sqrt W\tanh(\phi(z)^\top\btheta/\sqrt W)$,
143: with $\|\phi(z)\|_2\le1$ and projected parameters $\|\btheta\|_2\le1$.
144: Contexts have dimension four, there are five actions, and the context--action
145: feature map has dimension 29.  Noise has standard deviation $0.25$, the metric
146: ridge is one, and the confidence parameter is $\delta=0.05$.
147: A fixed teacher generates the rewards.  The conditions were specified before
148: their evaluation outcomes were observed.  Development, tuning, and evaluation
149: use disjoint seed sets.
150: 
151: The shared optimizer uses learning rate $3\times10^{-4}$ with 20 full-batch
152: steps followed by projection each round.  It was selected from nine
153: candidates by prediction MSE on uniform-random tuning histories.  This fixes
154: one implementation choice across policies; it does not establish
155: policy-specific regret-optimal tuning.  Dense float64 matrices and Cholesky
156: solves implement the exact-operator abstraction.  Actions are enumerated,
157: with ties resolved by the smallest action index.  This 29-parameter study
158: therefore examines dense numerical implementations.  It does not test
159: approximate solvers, large-model scalability, or real-data performance.
160: \Cref{app:transport-followup} records the protocol and provenance.
161: 
162: \paragraph{What do the recorded decisions reveal?}
163: After observing the policy outcomes, we examined how the Hessian score's
164: width bonus related to its recommendations.  We independently recomputed score
165: diagnostics from all 600 preserved trajectories.  On Hessian's own histories,
166: its selected action equals the current-width argmax on 99.382\%, 99.962\%, and 99.982\% of
167: rounds for $W=16,1,0.25$.  A stronger sufficient condition---the bonus gap
168: between the two largest widths exceeding the entire range of prediction
169: centers---holds on 97.104\%, 99.372\%, and 99.508\% of rounds.
170: Under this condition, differences in predicted reward cannot overturn the
171: largest-width action's bonus advantage.  Argmax agreement means that the
172: policy chooses the action ranked first by current width under the same tie
173: rule.  The stronger condition identifies states where the bonus gap alone
174: forces that choice.  The rounds are dependent, and this retrospective
175: calculation does not identify an adaptive causal mechanism.
176: 
177: The per-seed table in \Cref{app:transport-followup} evaluates this same Hessian
178: score on histories generated by all four policies.  Its non-Hessian rows
179: describe what Hessian would recommend on those states, not how the other
180: policies' own scores choose actions.  The appendix also compares alternative
181: recommendations while holding a recorded history fixed and checks sensitivity
182: to early numerical rankings.  Changing a recommendation in such a calculation
183: does not reveal the later observations or decisions of a policy that actually
184: took that action.
185: 
186: \paragraph{How tight are the endpoint certificates on recorded states?}
187: The relative-weight construction in \Cref{cor:tanh-relative-weights} permits
188: uniform and category-specific endpoint comparisons without using the Hessian
189: path envelope.  After observing the outcomes, we audit these comparisons on
190: the same 600 recorded histories, replaying representation updates with the
191: recorded actions and rewards.  On primary histories, the category-specific
192: outward factor gives mean
193: effective-width overheads of $0.28\%$--$12.68\%$ relative to the direct reference
194: width, versus $0.16\%$--$12.13\%$ for the dense endpoint factor across conditions
195: (\Cref{app:transport-followup}).  These are means of actionwise ratios, not
196: ratios of mean widths: each effective width is compared with its reference
197: width before averaging.
198: 
199: This calculation shows the size of the certificate overhead on existing
200: states.  It evaluates neither a new adaptive policy nor end-to-end speed.
